narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 54.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Even though many accepted students sit around the middle of their class (roughly 6th decile), you ranked in the bottom decile in both your first and third years. These unusually low rankings outweighed everything else in the model’s eyes.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.80 worked in the opposite direction. It is well above the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction noticeably toward passing. However, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 37, family income in the upper-middle bracket, and plan to attend full-time are all very close to the typical profile of accepted students, so they had little influence on the outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic standing in law school. Stronger performance in future coursework that lifts your class rank would likely change the model’s prediction and open the door to admission on a later application. Consider seeking academic support early and tracking your progress against your peers each semester.
